t: How to NOT Freak Out about the Common Core
q: And when something like the Common Core State Standards (CCSS) come out, our frontal lobes, already overwhelmed by parents and deadlines and IEPs and ACTs and AYP, delegate to our brain stems, and our brain stems immediately shift us into fight-or-flight mode.
Once you've chosen the most crucial standards, it's empowerment time: ignore the rest of them while you, your students, and your colleagues work on dominating the few you chose.

In my professional opinion, the only way to sensibly use these standards is to focus on a few, master them, and, only when mastered, move on from there. Bluntly, the professional thing to do is start by purposefully ignoring a majority of the CCSS. We should not be moving on to new things when we haven't yet demonstrably mastered the most important, basic things.
Seriously: standards are pointless if they merely garnish lesson plans, and that's all they will do if we give in to unreasonable pressures that say, “Master them all now.

In short: apply both flight and fight modes to the CCSS; fly from all but the most important, and fight pressures that tell you otherwise. Take the standards and make them meaningful for your setting.

The process for choosing where to start with the CCSS took our building's social studies professional learning community (PLC) about 15 minutes. When we began the process below, most of us had never read a word of the CCSS before.
Why? Because instead of being freaked out by the CCSS, our PLC now owns them. We've made them manageable and meaningful to us and our goals for our students.
x: Stuart diagnoses the two common teacher reactions to the Common Core, fighting it or avoiding it, as brain-stem fight-or-flight responses from educators already overloaded by parents, deadlines, IEPs and testing.

His counterproposal, the 'non-freaked out approach', is to choose two or three standards a team judges most important for college and career readiness and deliberately ignore the rest until those are mastered.
His core move is deliberate neglect: focus on two or three high-leverage standards, master them, and only then move on, treating purposeful ignoring as the professional choice.
He argues that standards imposed all at once only garnish lesson plans, so teachers should fight pressure to 'master them all now' with Schmoker's Focus in hand.
He recasts fight-or-flight productively: flee from all but the most important standards and fight the pressure to master everything now.

The practical center is a fifteen-minute protocol his social studies PLC used to settle on close reading (R.CCR.1) and text-based argument (W.CCR.1), followed by experimenting, sharing results and discussing.
The payoff he claims is ownership: the team now owns standards it once had not even read.

t: How To Sweep Excitability Out Of Your Classroom https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2013/01/26/how-to-sweep-excitability-out-of-your-classroom/
q: The classroom teacher, however, is in the dark—the last to know. He (or she) is acutely aware of his struggles with classroom management, to be sure, and can clearly see how excitable and prone his students are to trouble.
This phenomenon is one of the most common causes of misbehavior, but it can be hard to recognize in your own classroom.
He or she must calm racing hearts, dissipate nervous energy, and restore peace to the classroom before starting the lesson.

Leading your students with clarity and conviction, speaking softly but confidently, responding to misbehavior with grace and aplomb . . . your calm assurance will settle over your students like a Scottish fog.
Simply ask for your students’ attention, and for the next 30 seconds or so just breathe—slowly and deeply. Don’t say a word. Don’t move around the room. Be still.
Wait for shoulders to relax, furrowed brows to slacken, and appreciative eyes to rest on you.
x: Specialist teachers who see a class only occasionally often instinctively calm students before teaching, offering a model to imitate.
A teacher's own tension and hurriedness can be an invisible root cause of classroom excitability and misbehavior.
He points to specialist teachers, like music or art teachers, who instinctively calm a class before starting a lesson, as a model for restoring peace.
This calm energy, he argues, settles over students and prepares them to learn.

The remedy he prescribes is a deliberate slowing down: carrying oneself with unhurried purpose, pausing to breathe silently with the class for about 30 seconds, and following it with a lighthearted story or joke.
Linsin explains that a teacher's own stress and hurriedness often causes the very excitability and misbehavior they struggle to control, even though it is hard to notice from inside the daily grind.

t: Why Forgiveness Is A Powerful Classroom Management Strategy management-strategy/
q: The decisions you make in the seconds after these feelings hit separate those who struggle with classroom management and those who excel.
You need a moment to take a deep breath and remind yourself that reacting emotionally is always a mistake.
Forgiveness, you see, in the form of complete and radical absolution of any and all past misbehavior—no matter how egregious—is a powerful classroom management strategy.
It has the power to soothe bitter, vengeful hearts, melt away heavily fortified walls of distrust, and turn your most challenging students into everyday members of your class.
You must show them through your quick smile and open, welcoming body language that every day is a new day and that the mistakes of the past are truly forgotten and gone forever.
Although forgiveness is a gift on the house, what you receive in return can be reason to springboard wide-eyed out of bed every morning.
x: Linsin describes forgiveness as a deliberate classroom management strategy, not just a personal virtue, that separates teachers who excel at managing behavior from those who struggle.
A moment of pause before reacting to misbehavior prevents emotional overreaction and becomes an ingrained habit over time.

Radical, no-strings-attached forgiveness can turn the most challenging students into everyday, contributing class members.
Forgiveness must be actively shown to students, not just felt internally, through warmth, smiles, and a fresh start each day.

t: Simple Rubrics for Common Core Speaking and Listening Standards
q: While my speaking and listening rubrics for the CCSS aren't going to win me a gold star in an Ed Theory class, they do effectively tell me whether my students have it, are on the way to getting it, or are showing no evidence of getting it. In other words, they may not be sexy, but they work.

To help illustrate why and how they're working on this move, I also connect the Speaking and Listening move to moves I want them to make in their writing. Speaking and Listening tasks are awesome avenues into better writing and reading.

To scaffold the moves, I often include a sentence starter or two on the board (energetic nod to Graff and Birkenstein). These enable students to frame their ideas within effective language. I always remind students that their responses need not be limited to these templates.

My goal with grading Speaking and Listening standards is to give students feedback that is immediate (I'm done grading them by the time they sit down), focused (hence giving them one skill per speaking task), and, ultimately, helpful to them. At the end of the day, my students are the ones that will live with their speaking and listening abilities — not me.

Just this past week, I had a student tell me about how she spoke up at a community event one evening, and that she did so because of the confidence she has gained in my class. For the first two months of school, I couldn't get this kid to speak loud enough to be heard a few feet away.

Mandatory participation (even for shy kids) is possible in my room because I strive to build community from Day 1, and because my students know that I am an equal opportunity comfort zone destroyer. I also share with them about how I was super shy in high school, and how that shyness has only been harder to overcome as an adult.

Even though the Speaking and Listening standard is technically only for ELA classes, my students and I probably tend to do just as much Speaking and Listening work in my World History classes as in my Freshman Comp/Lit classes. To me, social studies classes seem like they should be filled with chances to discuss and debate.
x: His check / check-minus / zero scoring is deliberately crude, justified by what it tells him: whether a student has the skill, is on the way, or shows no evidence.

Each oral skill is explained, modeled on a different topic and scaffolded with a sentence starter, and explicitly linked to a parallel move in writing, making discussion an on-ramp to better reading and writing.

For any graded debate or discussion, students are given a single Speaking and Listening skill, which he explains, models on a different topic and scaffolds with sentence starters borrowed from Graff and Birkenstein's…
Grading is a new roster column scored check, check-minus or zero, so feedback is immediate, focused and finished by the time students sit down.

He defends mandatory participation for shy students with an anecdote of a girl who went from inaudible to speaking at a community event, attributing it to deliberate community-building from the first day.

A frequently-asked-questions section carries the rest of the argument: mandatory participation, even for students reduced to tears, is possible because he builds community from day one and is open about his own shyness.
Stuart argues Speaking and Listening work belongs just as much in social studies as in ELA, running as many debates in World History as in his composition and literature classes.

t: Why You Should Handle Your Own Behavior Problems problems/
q: But in the long run, sending students to the office makes managing your classroom more difficult. It also puts your administrator in the difficult position of trying to do for you what you can more effectively do yourself.
You see, when you send students to the office for misbehavior, you’re making a clear statement to your class that you’re not the ultimate authority of your classroom.
The more you send students to the office, the more you’ll find yourself threatening, giving reminders and chances, and trying to persuade and even plead for your students to behave.
They’re left with using their title and authority to try and convince or intimidate students into behaving for you.
Being seen as the leader and decision maker of your classroom will engender greater respect and admiration from your students.
No matter how easy it may seem in the moment, no matter how satisfying it may be to remove a student from your classroom, it’s a mistake to send students to the office.
x: Linsin argues that sending misbehaving students to the office, though common, ultimately undermines a teacher's authority and makes classroom management harder in the long run.
Sending students to the office signals to the whole class that the teacher isn't the ultimate authority, inviting more testing of limits.
Frequent office referrals correlate with more threatening, reminding, and pleading rather than firm follow-through.

t: How To Manage Whole-Class Behavior While Working With A Small Group -working-with-a-small-group/
q: No, to fix it, you have to go back to the root cause of the problem.
In this case, the students outside the small group are misbehaving because they’re unprepared to work independently, and thus don’t do it well.
Your class must first prove that they can work on their own—under your observing eye—for at least the length of time you wish to meet with small groups.
You have to show them through directed teaching and modeling that once the lesson has been taught, the responsibility for learning shifts in total from you to them.
Many students have such deeply ingrained learned helplessness that it can take three or four weeks before your class is ready for you to begin working with small groups.
It’s okay and a good idea to periodically peek up from your small group to make sure all is well.
x: Chronic interruptions during small-group time stem from a root cause: students aren't yet prepared to work independently.
Once students prove they can work independently under observation, teachers can pull small groups without constant interruption, periodically glancing up to verify all is well.

He warns that shifting full responsibility for learning onto students, and weaning them off constant teacher availability, can take three to four weeks for classes with deep learned helplessness.
